sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Python Pandas Tutorial

steps.title: Install pandas and load CSV
steps.instructions: Run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into the folder, then in main.py import pandas as pd, read orders.csv into df and print(df). Run `uv run main.py` to see the table ending in [40 rows x 9 columns].

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
The printed table ends with its row/column count

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip / pip3
Using uv to create a virtual environment and add pandas
Why pandas is imported as pd
DataFrames vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data (rows and columns)
pd.read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Reading the printed DataFrame: 40 rows and 9 columns

hints: Make sure pandas is installed in your project: run `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`).
Put orders.csv in the same folder you run the script from, then load it with `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`.
Add `print(df)` and run the file with `uv run main.py`; the last line should read like `[40 rows x 9 columns]`.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, giving ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
orders.csv not in the working directory, causing FileNotFoundError.
Saving the GitHub page HTML instead of the raw CSV, so the shape is wrong or parsing fails.
Typing `pd.read.csv` or `pd.readcsv` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Forgetting `print(df)`, so nothing appears when running a plain .py file.
Naming the script pandas.py, which shadows the real pandas module.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load data in Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb (Cmd+Shift+P > New Jupyter Notebook); in cell 1 import pandas as pd and read orders.csv into df, then print(df) in cell 2.

targets.caption: New Jupyter notebook saved as notebook.ipynb
First cell: import pandas and load orders.csv into df
Second cell: print the DataFrame

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P > New Jupyter Notebook
Python extension is required for notebooks in VS Code
Cells can be run independently; data stays loaded
Running, deleting cells and clearing outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P), choose "Create: New Jupyter Notebook", and save it as notebook.ipynb next to orders.csv.
In the first cell write `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`, then run it and pick a Python kernel that has pandas installed.
Add a new cell below with `print(df)` and run just that cell. The table should appear under it.
If you see ModuleNotFoundError, install pandas into the kernel you selected. If you see FileNotFoundError, make sure orders.csv is in the same folder as the notebook.
common_mistakes: No Python extension installed in VS Code, so the New Jupyter Notebook command is missing
Selecting a kernel/interpreter that doesn't have pandas installed (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas')
orders.csv not in the notebook's folder, causing FileNotFoundError
Running the print(df) cell before the read_csv cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined
Typing pd.readcsv instead of pd.read_csv
steps.run_command: Run cell 1, then run cell 2 (select a Python kernel when prompted)
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info() and df.describe() in cells, then inspect df.columns and df.index.

targets.caption: Preview the first five rows
Column names, types and entry count
Summary statistics for numeric columns
The row index as a RangeIndex

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entries, columns and dtypes; why strings show as object
describe() generates descriptive statistics
df.columns lists column names
df.index is a RangeIndex (start, stop, step)

hints: Make sure the cell that loads your CSV into df has been run first, so df exists.
Put each of head(), tail(), info() and describe() in its own cell so you can see each output.
head, tail, info and describe are methods and need parentheses; columns and index are attributes and do not.
df.info() prints a summary starting with 'RangeIndex: N entries'. df.index should show RangeIndex(start=0, stop=N, step=1).
common_mistakes: Running these cells before the cell with pd.read_csv, which gives NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError: 'Index' object is not callable.
Forgetting parentheses on df.head or df.describe, which prints a bound method instead of a table.
Expecting describe() to summarize text columns: by default it only covers numeric columns.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: In your notebook, select a column with df['Country'] and several with df[['Country', 'Product']]. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]['Country'].

targets.caption: Select one column, which returns a Series
A list of columns returns a DataFrame
Select a row by position with iloc
Get one value from a row by its column name

explanations.topic: Indexing a single column returns a pandas Series
Using plain Python functions on a column: len and set
A list of columns returns a DataFrame
iloc selects rows by integer position
Pandas data types differ from built-in Python types
Access a row's values by position or by column name

hints: Run df.columns first to see the exact column names you can use.
One column uses single brackets, for example df['Country']. Several columns need a list inside the brackets, for example df[['Country', 'Product']].
Rows are selected with df.iloc[n]. Chain a column name onto the result to get one value: df.iloc[10]['Country'].
If you get a KeyError, the column name is misspelled or has the wrong capitalization. Copy it from the df.columns output.
common_mistakes: Writing df['Country', 'Product'] with single brackets instead of passing a list. This raises a KeyError.
Getting the capitalization or spacing of a column name wrong, for example 'country' instead of 'Country'.
Using df[0] to get a row. That looks for a column named 0, so use df.iloc[0] instead.
Writing df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of square brackets.
Forgetting that iloc starts at 0, so df.iloc[10] is the 11th row.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with combined conditions using & and |, plus a numeric comparison. Use .str.startswith(...) and ~df[...].isin([...]) to filter by text and membership.

targets.caption: Wrap each condition in parentheses and join with & (and) or | (or)
String methods via the .str accessor
isin checks membership in a list; ~ negates it

explanations.topic: Boolean mask filtering with df[condition]
Combining conditions with & and parentheses
Using | for or conditions
Comparison operators on numeric columns
.str string methods like startswith/endswith
isin and the ~ negation operator

hints: Filtering means putting a True/False condition inside df[...].
Each condition in a combined filter must be wrapped in its own parentheses, e.g. (df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA').
String checks go through .str: df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')].
For 'not in a list', put ~ before the condition: df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])].
common_mistakes: Filtering on the wrong column (e.g. 'Product' instead of 'Category') and getting an empty table.
Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises a ValueError about ambiguous truth value.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |.
Calling .startswith directly on the Series without .str.
Case mismatch in string matching, e.g. endswith('A') instead of endswith('a').
Passing separate arguments to isin instead of a single list.
steps.code:
df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') | (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[df['Quantity'] > 2]
df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')]
df[df['CustomerName'].str.endswith('a')]
df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]
df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]

steps.title: Update values with loc
steps.instructions: Update values with df.loc[condition, 'Column'] = new_value. Uppercase a column with df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().

targets.caption: Locate rows by condition, then pick the column to update
Uppercase every value in a column
Updated values shown in the output

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label/condition vs iloc by index position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame since multiple rows may match
Adding a column after the comma to assign a new value
Replacing all USA entries with United States in one assignment
Using .str.upper() to transform a whole column

hints: Use df.loc[condition, 'ColumnName'] = new_value to update the matching rows.
The condition is a boolean Series like df['Country'] == 'USA'. Put it inside the loc brackets, then a comma, then the column name.
After assigning, run df.loc[condition] or df[condition] in a new cell to confirm the change.
To uppercase a column, reassign it: df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
common_mistakes: Using chained indexing like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ... This doesn't update df and raises SettingWithCopyWarning.
Misspelling the column name (e.g. 'ProductName' instead of 'Product'). With loc this silently creates a new column.
Writing .string.upper() or .upper() directly on the Series instead of .str.upper().
Forgetting to assign the result back: df['Country'].str.upper() alone does not modify df.
Re-running the USA filter after uppercasing and expecting matches. The values are now 'UNITED STATES'.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with df = df.drop(39), check df.tail(), then use dropna() and fillna(..., inplace=True). Rename a column with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True) and display df.

targets.caption: Drop the row at index 39 and reassign to df
Confirm the dropped row is gone
Fill missing values in place instead of dropping them
Rename OrderID to 'Order ID'

explanations.topic: df.drop(39) removes the row with index label 39; reassigning keeps the change
dropna removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing rows
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns={...})

hints: drop, dropna, fillna and rename return a new DataFrame unless you reassign it (df = ...) or pass inplace=True.
To remove one row use df = df.drop(<index label>), then call df.tail() to check it.
Rename with a dict mapping old name to new name: df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True).
If drop raises a KeyError, the label isn't in the index. Pick one that is listed in df.tail() or df.index.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning to df, so the row seems to come back.
Running the drop cell twice, which gives KeyError because label 39 is already gone.
Using a column name in rename that doesn't exactly match the existing one (case or spacing), so nothing changes and no error is shown.
Writing df = df.fillna(..., inplace=True), which sets df to None.
Expecting dropna() to change df when it isn't reassigned and has no inplace=True.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

df.dropna()

df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save data
steps.instructions: Run df['Country'].value_counts(), df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum() and df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False). Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).

targets.caption: Count how often each country appears
Sum prices per country
Sort rows by price, highest first
Save the modified DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts counts occurrences of each unique value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY: aggregate a column per group
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv saves the DataFrame; index=False omits the index column

hints: Each operation goes in its own notebook cell. Run them one at a time with Shift+Enter.
Count values with df['Country'].value_counts(). Group with df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum().
Sort with df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False).
Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False). The new file should then appear in your file browser.
common_mistakes: Writing value_count() or valuecounts() instead of value_counts().
Calling .sum without parentheses, which shows a method object instead of the totals.
Passing ascending='False' as a string, or forgetting it and getting ascending order.
Writing df.2csv or to_CSV instead of to_csv.
Column names that don't match the CSV exactly (e.g. 'country' vs 'Country'), causing a KeyError.
Forgetting index=False, so an extra unnamed index column is written to the file.
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
